questions.q: Match each part of a candle to what it shows.
pairs: From the open to the close
questions.why: A candle packs open, high, low and close for one period into one shape.

questions.q: A candle opens at 50, falls to 44, rises to 51 and closes at 46. What kind of candle is it?
options: A down candle: body from 50 to 46, wicks to 51 and 44
An up candle: body from 46 to 50
A down candle: body from 51 to 44
An up candle with no wicks
questions.why: It closed below its open, so it's a down candle. Body = open to close; wicks = high and low.

options: One big rise in a day
questions.why: An uptrend makes higher highs and higher lows; a downtrend the opposite; a range moves sideways.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A level where falls have repeatedly stopped
A level where rises have repeatedly stalled
Price pushing clearly through a level
Poking through a level then falling back
questions.why: Levels show where buyers or sellers have acted before, not guarantees.

questions.q: After a price breaks above resistance, that old resistance level often acts as support.
questions.why: Old resistance often becomes new support (and vice versa), though not always.

questions.q: You buy near support at 100. Where does a stop-loss usually make most sense?
questions.why: The stop goes where you'd be proved wrong: just beyond the level that should have held.

questions.q: Put these chart timeframes in order from most noise to the biggest picture.
questions.why: Shorter timeframes show more random wiggles; longer ones show the main trend.

questions.q: A price that has bounced off a level three times will definitely bounce the fourth time.
questions.why: Nothing is definite. Repeated bounces suggest buyers have been active there, but levels break often.

questions.q: You buy at {e} with a stop at {s} and a target at the next resistance, {t}. What's the reward-to-risk ratio? (e.g. 2 for 2:1)
Explain why support and resistance levels might work, at least some of the time.

ideas.label: Traders remember prices: buyers who missed out or sellers wanting to get out even act at the same levels
Many traders watch the same levels, so their orders can make it self-fulfilling

questions.model: People remember prices: buyers who missed out at a low may buy if it returns, and people who bought at a high may sell to get out even when it comes back. And because many traders watch the same levels and place orders there, the effect can become partly self-fulfilling.
questions.why: Memory and crowd behaviour, not magic.

tests.answer: Traders remember previous prices and want to get out even, and because many traders watch the same levels it's self-fulfilling.
Because lots of traders place orders there.
Because the price can't go lower.

questions.q: Explain why chart patterns can look far more reliable than they really are.

ideas.label: Hindsight: on old charts you know what happened next
Random prices also make patterns, and failures get forgotten (need testing on many examples)

questions.model: On old charts you know what happened next, so successful patterns stand out and failures are forgotten. Random prices also form trends and patterns by chance. The only way to know is to test a pattern on many examples, including the failures.
questions.why: Hindsight and randomness make charts persuasive.

tests.answer: With hindsight you already know what happened, and random noise makes patterns while you forget the failures.
